paragraphs: BiMark addresses three goals for watermarking language-model output: preserving the quality of generated text, detecting the watermark without relying on a particular model, and embedding a message containing multiple bits. The central difficulty is that increasing the amount of embedded information can interfere with text quality. The paper develops a framework intended to meet these goals together.

Its design combines three mechanisms. A bit-flip reweighting procedure provides unbiased watermarking and supports model-agnostic detection. A multilayer structure strengthens detectability while preserving generation quality. An information-encoding component lets the watermark carry multiple bits, extending its role beyond a simple indication that text has been watermarked.

Theoretical analysis and experiments support the framework. Against existing multi-bit methods, the authors report extraction rates up to 30% higher for short texts, alongside lower perplexity as an indicator of text quality. On summarization and translation, performance is comparable to non-watermarked text. These results suggest that stronger message recovery and useful downstream behavior can coexist in the evaluated settings.
icml-2025-bimark-unbiased-multilayer-wat.tldr: BiMark combines unbiased reweighting, multiple watermark layers, and message encoding to improve short-text watermark recovery while preserving text quality.

paragraphs: Preference-based reinforcement learning often asks people which of two trajectories they prefer. That answer supplies an ordering, but offers limited direct information about how strongly one option is preferred. When trajectories differ only subtly, making the comparison can also be difficult. This paper changes the question asked of the person providing feedback.

A distinguishability query presents two pairs of trajectories. The labeler first chooses the pair whose members are easier to distinguish, then states a preference within that easier pair. Comparing the pairs conveys information about preference strength, while choosing the clearer comparison is expected to reduce cognitive effort. The authors connect this feedback to cardinal utility and relations between utility differences.

The paper also develops a query-selection procedure that balances how informative a question is against how easy it is to answer. Experiments show potential for faster, more data-efficient learning and improved usability on RLHF benchmarks. The reported benefits are particularly relevant to classical control settings, where the strength of preferences matters for maximizing expected utility.
icml-2025-comparing-comparisons-informat.tldr: Asking people which of two trajectory pairs is easier to distinguish can reveal preference strength and support more efficient feedback collection.

paragraphs: Heavy ball momentum is well studied for minimizing a single objective, but its behavior in min-max games is less understood. These games involve competing optimization directions, making familiar intuition from minimization potentially misleading. The paper studies momentum through continuous-time analysis, considering both simultaneous updates and updates that alternate between the competing sides.

The local analysis finds that smaller momentum improves stability by allowing convergence over a wider range of step sizes. Alternating updates generally converge faster in this analysis. This connects the momentum choice to both whether nearby trajectories converge and how quickly they do so, rather than treating momentum simply as an acceleration mechanism.

The global analysis examines implicit regularization: how the optimization procedure influences the regions it visits. Smaller momentum directs trajectories toward regions with shallower slopes, and alternating updates strengthen this tendency. The authors contrast these findings with minimization, where larger momentum produces similar effects. Numerical experiments support the theory, highlighting why momentum choices for min-max problems need their own analysis.
icml-2025-continuous-time-analysis-of-he.tldr: Continuous-time analysis finds that smaller heavy ball momentum improves local stability and favors shallower slopes in min-max games.

paragraphs: RGB-X tracking combines ordinary color images with another modality, such as depth, thermal measurements, or event data. Many trackers process the two streams in separate branches. The paper argues that maintaining these separate feature spaces complicates computation, while modeling spatial relationships within each stream consumes resources that could support interaction between modalities and tracking over time.

CSTrack brings the streams into a compact representation. Its Spatial Compact Module integrates RGB and the additional input into a shared spatial feature, supporting relationships both within each modality and across modalities. Its Temporal Compact Module represents information over time through a refined heatmap describing the target distribution.

The two modules address complementary parts of tracking: combining spatial evidence from different sensors and retaining useful temporal information. The authors report that extensive experiments validate this compact approach and produce new state-of-the-art results on mainstream RGB-X benchmarks. The findings support compact spatiotemporal representation as an effective way to organize multimodal tracking, with the claimed gains demonstrated on those benchmarks.
icml-2025-cstrack-enhancing-rgb-x-tracki.tldr: CSTrack combines multimodal spatial features and compact temporal heatmaps to achieve state-of-the-art results on RGB-X tracking benchmarks.

paragraphs: The sparse-group lasso selects both individual variables and groups of variables. This is useful when high-dimensional data contain meaningful groupings, as often happens in genetics. Its flexibility brings computational costs, however: the combined penalty makes coefficient shrinkage more complex, and an additional hyperparameter must be tuned. The paper targets the work required to fit these models.

Dual Feature Reduction reduces the input space before optimization. It uses strong screening rules for both the standard sparse-group lasso and its adaptive variant. Two screening layers draw on dual norms and subdifferentials, mathematical tools associated with the penalty and its optimization conditions. The stated goal is to remove unnecessary optimization work without changing solution optimality.

Studies on synthetic and real data show large computational savings across many scenarios. The significance is that the method accelerates an existing modeling approach while retaining its variable-selection and group-selection purpose. Users can therefore benefit from the sparse-group formulation without having every fitting problem carry the full original input space through optimization.
icml-2025-dual-feature-reduction-for-the.tldr: Dual Feature Reduction screens the inputs to sparse-group lasso models before optimization, reducing computational cost without affecting solution optimality.

paragraphs: Training spiking neural networks can be slow because their dynamics are processed sequentially over time. With T timesteps, this creates a time complexity that grows as O(T). Fixed-point Parallel Training addresses that temporal dependence while keeping the network architecture unchanged and, according to the paper, introducing no additional assumptions.

The method rewrites Leaky Integrate-and-Fire neuron dynamics as a fixed-point iteration covering all timesteps. This allows the temporal computation to be handled through K iterations, yielding the stated O(K) time complexity, where K is a small constant and is usually three. The authors analyze convergence and show that existing parallel spiking neurons fit within this formulation as special cases.

Experiments indicate that the method reproduces the dynamics of the original neurons while substantially reducing computation time without sacrificing accuracy. Its value is especially clear for long simulations, where sequential processing becomes increasingly expensive. The contribution combines a general formulation for parallel training with theoretical convergence analysis and empirical evidence that the acceleration preserves useful network behavior.
icml-2025-efficient-parallel-training-me.tldr: Fixed-point Parallel Training accelerates spiking networks by replacing sequential temporal processing with a small number of parallel fixed-point iterations.

paragraphs: Language models can sometimes answer questions about implications of newly finetuned facts, even when those implications were not directly supplied during finetuning. This paper proposes extractive structures as a framework for explaining how model components cooperate to produce that behavior. The focus is on both where a fact is stored and how other components make use of it.

Within the framework, informative components record facts through changes in their weights. Extractive components before and after them query and process that information to produce an implication. The authors hypothesize that pretraining develops these structures when implications appear after facts the model already knows. This predicts an ordering effect and the possibility of transferring structures through weight grafting to obtain counterfactual implications.

Experiments demonstrate these effects in OLMo-7b, Llama 3-8b, Gemma 2-9b, and Qwen 2-7b. These observations support the proposed mechanism without turning the pretraining hypothesis into a universal explanation. The results also indicate that facts can be learned in early or late layers, with different resulting forms of generalization.
icml-2025-extractive-structures-learned-.tldr: The paper proposes and empirically investigates cooperating model components that let pretrained language models derive implications from finetuned facts.

paragraphs: Graph World Model aims to bring graph structure and multimodal information into a single world-model framework. The paper identifies a gap between world models centered on unstructured data and graph foundation models centered on graph-learning tasks. Its approach supports both graph-structured and unstructured states, while representing different tasks as actions within the model.

The core operation passes messages to aggregate information across structure. One version, GWM-T, converts multimodal data into text and works in a common token space. Another, GWM-E, uses modality-specific encoders to create a common embedding space. Action nodes connect tasks to other nodes through direct references or computed similarities, allowing the same framework to express different operations.

Across evaluations spanning generation, matching, recommendation, graph prediction, and other domains, the authors report performance matching or exceeding domain-specific baselines. They also find benefits from multihop structure and strong zero-shot or few-shot performance on unseen tasks. These findings support the usefulness of a shared structured representation for tasks usually addressed by separate specialized models.
icml-2025-graph-world-model-09d2d41851.tldr: Graph World Model uses message passing and action nodes to handle diverse tasks over graph-structured and unstructured multimodal information.

paragraphs: Neural operators offer a way to solve high-dimensional partial differential equations, but some problems require more than satisfying the governing equation. Their solutions must also obey equality or inequality constraints. HEAP addresses this constrained setting, where an effective learned solver must account for these additional requirements as part of its computation.

The authors formulate learning the evolution operator as a quadratic programming problem. They then incorporate the steps of an adaptive primal-dual hybrid gradient algorithm into the neural operator architecture. This process, called unrolling, makes the optimization procedure part of the network's structure. The learned operator evolves in the parameter space of the differential equations.

This design links neural computation to a constrained optimization method, with the stated benefit of improved efficiency while retaining theoretical guarantees from that optimization. Experiments on a variety of high-dimensional equations show HEAP outperforming a state-of-the-art neural operator model. The contribution is therefore an architectural route for incorporating constraints, supported by both an optimization formulation and empirical comparisons.
icml-2025-heap-hyper-extended-a-pdhg-ope.tldr: HEAP embeds an adaptive constrained-optimization algorithm into a neural operator for solving high-dimensional partial differential equations.

paragraphs: A sketch summarizes a potentially unending data stream using limited memory, allowing item frequencies to be estimated without retaining the whole stream. Neural sketches learn how to compress this information using memory-augmented networks. The paper identifies a practical obstacle: fixed network configurations make existing neural sketches difficult to adapt to different data domains and memory budgets.

Lego Sketch introduces a modular memory architecture. It dynamically coordinates multiple memory bricks, allowing the sketch to adjust how it uses storage across different space budgets and data domains. The important design choice is to make the memory organization adaptable, so the neural approach can scale beyond one rigid configuration.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and empirical studies supporting both scalability and improved trade-offs between memory use and estimation accuracy. They report better results than existing handcrafted and neural sketches. This matters because a useful streaming summary must remain accurate under a storage constraint, and the appropriate constraint can differ substantially between applications. Lego Sketch directly targets that adaptability alongside accuracy.
icml-2025-lego-sketch-a-scalable-memory-.tldr: Lego Sketch coordinates modular memory units to improve streaming frequency estimation across different data domains and memory budgets.

paragraphs: Federated telemetry collects information from distributed devices, but protecting transmitted results does not by itself address exposure of a device's internal state. This paper studies local pan-privacy, which asks for privacy to survive repeated, unannounced intrusions into that local state. The concrete task is to monitor how often an event occurs while hiding individual local occurrences even from an intruder on the affected device.

The authors first establish a limit on what can be achieved. Under the constraints considered in the paper, information-theoretic differential privacy against these intrusions is incompatible with collecting telemetry information. This is a conditional impossibility result: the conflict concerns that privacy requirement within the stated setting, rather than every conceivable form of private telemetry.

The paper then shows that standard cryptographic primitives enable a scalable solution. The distinction matters because it identifies both an obstacle and a way forward. Protecting telemetry against local-state compromise requires carefully choosing the kind of privacy protection sought; cryptographic techniques make useful collection possible in the problem the authors study.
icml-2025-local-pan-privacy-for-federate.tldr: The paper establishes a conditional impossibility for information-theoretically private local telemetry under intrusion, then provides a scalable cryptographic solution.

paragraphs: Model Swarms adapts a collection of language-model experts through collaborative search. It begins with existing experts and a utility function expressing the desired adaptation objective. Instead of prescribing how particular experts should be combined, it lets the pool search through model weight space, using the best checkpoints discovered across models to guide subsequent movement.

The paper describes this as tuning-free adaptation and reports that it works with as few as 200 examples. It does not require assumptions about which experts the swarm contains or how they should be composed. This makes the search procedure applicable to different objectives expressed through the utility function, including individual tasks, multiple task domains, reward modeling, and human interests.

Experiments report improvements over 12 model-composition baselines, reaching up to 21.0% across evaluated tasks and contexts. Further analysis finds capabilities absent from the initial checkpoints and transitions from weaker to stronger experts during collaborative search. These are empirical findings about the studied swarms, supporting collaborative weight-space exploration as a flexible adaptation method.
icml-2025-model-swarms-collaborative-sea.tldr: Model Swarms adapts language-model experts through collaborative weight-space search guided by shared successful checkpoints and a utility function.

paragraphs: Multimodal object re-identification aims to retrieve a particular object using information from different modalities. MFRNet addresses two difficulties in combining that information: limited interaction among fine-grained features across modalities, and the challenge of preserving both shared information and features specific to each modality. Both matter for distinguishing the target object from other candidates.

The network separates these responsibilities into two components. Its Feature Fusion Module creates pixel-level features and enables flexible interaction across modalities. Its Feature Representation Module extracts and combines modality-specific and modality-shared features. Together, they aim to retain useful distinctions while making information from the different inputs work together, with little additional parameter overhead.

Experiments on RGBNT201, RGBNT100, and MSVR310 support improvements in accuracy and efficiency. On RGBNT201, the abstract reports improvements of 8.4% in mean average precision and 6.9% in accuracy, with negligible extra parameters. The findings suggest that better organization of feature fusion and representation can improve retrieval without requiring a large increase in model size.
icml-2025-multi-modal-object-re-identifi.tldr: MFRNet improves multimodal object retrieval by combining fine-grained cross-modal fusion with shared and modality-specific feature representations.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can detect industrial anomalies effectively, but repeated denoising steps make inference slow. OmiAD targets this obstacle by turning a multi-step diffusion model into a single-step generator for multiclass anomaly detection. Its approach combines a reconstruction strategy designed for anomalies with a compression procedure designed to preserve useful detection behavior.

The starting model adjusts masking patterns according to noise levels. Masking encourages it to use broader context when reconstructing abnormal regions as normal counterparts, reducing reliance on pixel-level shortcuts. The authors then apply Adversarial Score Distillation to compress the denoising process. This combines score distillation with a discriminator that shares weights, reusing parameters while improving efficiency and detection performance.

Evaluation on four diverse datasets reports state-of-the-art results across seven metrics and a substantial inference speedup. The stated result is therefore more than reducing the number of generation steps: the compressed system also performs strongly at detecting anomalies. This supports the combination of context-sensitive reconstruction and adversarial distillation for the industrial deployment problem motivating the work.
icml-2025-omiad-one-step-adaptive-masked.tldr: OmiAD distills an adaptively masked diffusion model into one-step anomaly detection, reporting faster inference and state-of-the-art detection results.

paragraphs: Randomized data structures can face difficulties when later queries depend on earlier answers, because responses may expose their internal randomness. Differential privacy has been used to protect that randomness and preserve correctness across adaptive queries. Earlier results addressed numerical estimates, including an optimization problem's cost. This paper studies returning an actual solution, which can reveal substantially more information.

The authors focus on nearest-neighbor search and regression under arbitrary turnstile updates. Their algorithms return a solution point or a solution vector, respectively. They identify problem-specific parameters that influence the required resources, including the number of approximately near neighbors and the matrix condition number, and apply different differential-privacy techniques to these search settings.

The resulting memory and time costs depend on those parameters, with related trade-offs obtained for both problems. The contribution extends privacy-based protection of internal randomness beyond scalar answers. It also shows why the richer output of a search query requires attention to the structure of the underlying problem when designing algorithms for repeated adaptive use.
icml-2025-on-differential-privacy-for-ad.tldr: The paper uses differential privacy to support adaptive nearest-neighbor and regression searches, with resource costs depending on key problem parameters.

paragraphs: Flow matching supports generative tasks ranging from images to decision-making, where generation often needs to follow an energy-based objective. The paper argues that guidance for general flow matching differs substantially from guidance in diffusion models. It develops a framework intended to cover this broader setting and derive guidance methods from a common foundation.

The framework yields several options. One is training-free guidance that is asymptotically exact. Others include new objectives for training guidance models and two classes of approximate guidance methods. Classical gradient-guidance procedures appear as special cases within those approximate classes. This distinguishes methods by their approximation properties and training requirements while connecting them mathematically.

The authors theoretically analyze the alternatives to help choose methods for different scenarios. Experiments on synthetic data, image inverse problems, and offline reinforcement learning support the effectiveness of the proposed techniques and the framework's correctness. The asymptotic qualification matters: the exactness claim concerns limiting behavior. Overall, the work supplies both new methods and a basis for understanding their relationships.
icml-2025-on-the-guidance-of-flow-matchi.tldr: A general framework for guiding flow-matching models derives training-free, learned, and approximate methods and analyzes their suitability across scenarios.

paragraphs: Precipitation nowcasting predicts how rainfall will develop over a sequence of future frames. Many methods train by minimizing mean squared error, but the paper argues that this can neglect constraints on the forecast distribution. The resulting predictions can have disappointing accuracy and image quality, especially farther into a forecast sequence. The proposed model adds perceptual constraints to address this issue.

The method formulates forecasting as a posterior mean-squared-error problem subject to those constraints. A precipitation estimator first produces posterior mean forecast sequences. Rectified flow then constructs a transformation between distributions. To give distant forecast frames more attention, the authors also introduce a frame-sampling strategy whose corresponding weights increase gradually.

The paper provides a theoretical argument for the reliability of its solution and evaluates it on two public radar datasets. It reports better performance than current state-of-the-art models in those experiments. The approach connects numerical forecast estimation with distributional constraints, while explicitly adjusting training emphasis toward the later frames that motivate much of the problem.
icml-2025-perceptually-constrained-preci.tldr: The model combines perceptual constraints, rectified flow, and increased emphasis on distant frames to improve precipitation nowcasting.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning from human feedback commonly uses a learned reward model to represent preferences. That model is an approximation because the underlying human values are not directly accessible. Improving behavior according to the approximation may therefore fail to consistently improve the underlying objective. PILAF addresses this issue through the choice of responses sent to humans for preference labeling.

Policy-Interpolated Learning for Aligned Feedback is a response-sampling strategy that explicitly connects preference learning with maximizing an underlying oracle reward. The intervention happens in feedback collection: the responses selected for labeling are part of the alignment method. This focuses attention on how preference data are obtained, as well as what reward model is learned from them.

The authors establish optimality from optimization and statistical perspectives within their theoretical treatment. They also report that the method is straightforward to implement and performs strongly in iterative and online RLHF settings. These findings support deliberate feedback curation as a useful component of aligning reward learning with the objective it is meant to represent.
icml-2025-pilaf-optimal-human-preference.tldr: PILAF selects responses for preference labeling to connect reward-model learning more directly with maximizing the underlying human reward.

paragraphs: Video diffusion transformers can require substantial storage and computation, creating obstacles for deployment on edge devices. Quantization reduces numerical precision to make models smaller and potentially faster, but methods developed for image generation transfer poorly to video. Q-VDiT addresses both information lost during quantization and optimization objectives that fail to account for video's temporal structure.

Its Token aware Quantization Estimator compensates for errors across token and feature dimensions. Temporal Maintenance Distillation addresses a different part of the problem: preserving relationships across space and time between frames. It allows each frame to be optimized in relation to the overall video, so compression takes the sequence context into account.

The reported W3A6 configuration achieves a scene-consistency score of 23.40, with a stated 1.9-fold advantage over current state-of-the-art quantization methods on that measure. This result supports tailoring compression to the dependencies within video generation. The contribution combines error compensation with a distillation objective that explicitly preserves connections among frames.
icml-2025-q-vdit-towards-accurate-quanti.tldr: Q-VDiT combines token-aware error compensation and temporal distillation to preserve video consistency when quantizing diffusion transformers.

paragraphs: Combinatorial optimization searches over discrete candidate solutions. This paper builds on discrete Langevin dynamics, a sampling approach that uses gradient information to guide that search. The authors observe that applying it directly can lead to insufficient exploration. Their proposed regularization addresses how far a newly sampled solution moves from the current one.

Regularized Langevin Dynamics enforces an expected distance between current and sampled solutions. This is intended to prevent overly local exploration and help avoid local minima. The authors use the same sampling framework to construct two solvers: one based on simulated annealing and another based on a neural network. The approach therefore supports both a traditional heuristic and a learned solver.

Experiments on three classic combinatorial problems show comparable or better performance than previous state-of-the-art solvers in the corresponding categories. The simulated-annealing version reduces runtime by up to 80% while matching or improving solution performance. These empirical results suggest that controlling sampling distance can make gradient-guided discrete search more effective across both solver styles.
icml-2025-regularized-langevin-dynamics-.tldr: Regularized Langevin Dynamics improves discrete search by controlling expected movement between solutions, benefiting simulated-annealing and neural solvers.

paragraphs: Targeted data selection chooses training examples to improve performance in a particular domain. TAROT addresses cases where that domain contains multiple distinct patterns. The paper argues that influence-based greedy methods can struggle here because dominant feature components distort influence estimates and linear additive selection assumptions fail to capture the richer distribution.

TAROT first uses whitened feature distance to reduce the disproportionate influence of dominant components. It then uses this distance within an optimal-transport objective, selecting data to reduce the distributional distance from the target domain. This makes matching the selected collection to the target distribution central to the selection process. The same minimization also helps estimate optimal selection ratios.

Experiments cover semantic segmentation, motion prediction, and instruction tuning, with consistently better results than state-of-the-art methods in the reported evaluations. These findings support the method across several kinds of deep-learning tasks. Its central contribution is to combine a less biased feature-distance measure with selection based on distribution matching, addressing both identified weaknesses of earlier heuristics.
icml-2025-tarot-targeted-data-selection-.tldr: TAROT selects training data by matching target distributions with optimal transport and whitened feature distances, improving results across several tasks.

paragraphs: This paper studies repeated play in zero-sum matrix games when players receive bandit feedback and learn without communicating. The goal is for their latest policies to converge to a Nash equilibrium. That requirement differs from convergence of an average over past policies: it asks the current state of play itself to approach equilibrium.

The authors establish that this last-iterate requirement carries a convergence-rate cost for uncoupled algorithms. They identify O(T^(-1/4)) as the best attainable rate in the studied setting, compared with the usual O(T^(-1/2)) rate for average iterates. This also improves on the previously available O(T^(-1/8)) bound on the exploitability gap described in the abstract.

Two proposed algorithms attain the optimal last-iterate rate. One uses a direct exploration–exploitation trade-off, while the other applies regularization through a two-step mirror-descent approach. Together, the lower-bound result and matching algorithms characterize the difficulty of the problem. They show both the cost of requiring convergence of current policies and how to meet that requirement at the optimal rate.
icml-2025-the-harder-path-last-iterate-c.tldr: For uncoupled zero-sum learning with bandit feedback, the paper establishes an optimal last-iterate rate of O(T^(-1/4)) and gives two matching algorithms.

paragraphs: Vision-language agents can produce textual actions that are subsequently processed into actions in an environment. This creates a difficult exploration problem for online reinforcement learning: the text space is large, and different textual changes can have very different effects on what the agent actually does. CoSo focuses exploration on the parts of generated text that influence those actions.

Counterfactual Soft Reinforcement Learning assesses the causal influence of individual tokens on the post-processed action. It then prioritizes exploration involving action-critical tokens while reducing the influence of redundant or low-impact tokens. This replaces uniform treatment of token uncertainty with a dynamic assessment tied to the agent's resulting behavior, making online rollouts more targeted.

The authors provide convergence and policy-improvement guarantees through theoretical analysis. Empirical evaluations on Android device control, card gaming, and embodied AI report better exploration efficiency and consistent performance gains. The findings support allocating exploration according to the consequences of textual choices, especially when action generation includes processing between model output and execution.
icml-2025-towards-efficient-online-tunin.tldr: CoSo improves online VLM-agent exploration by prioritizing generated tokens with greater causal influence on executed actions.

paragraphs: Post-training can refine language-model behavior and develop capabilities, but studying the role of synthetic data requires broad comparisons among data-generating models and model-based judges. The paper introduces WildChat-50M to make such large-scale comparisons more accessible. It expands the existing WildChat resource with responses from a much wider collection of models.

The dataset includes GPT responses alongside responses from more than 50 open-weight models, ranging from 0.5 billion to 104 billion parameters. This breadth supports comparative analysis across different sources of synthetic conversational data. The authors describe the dataset as the largest public chat dataset at the time of their work and conduct an extensive analysis using it.

They demonstrate its practical value by constructing Re-Wild, a public mixture for supervised finetuning. In the reported comparison, Re-Wild outperforms the Tulu-3 supervised-finetuning mixture while using only 40% as many samples. This result shows that the resource can support useful training-data curation, alongside its role in enabling research on synthetic responses and their evaluation.
icml-2025-wildchat-50m-a-deep-dive-into-.tldr: WildChat-50M broadens synthetic chat-data research and supports a finetuning mixture that outperforms Tulu-3's mixture with 40% as many samples.

paragraphs: Continual learning must accommodate new information while limiting the loss of previously learned capabilities. Many approaches rely on gradient-based updates, but gradients may be unavailable through black-box interfaces, constrained hardware, or non-differentiable systems. ZeroFlow addresses this setting with a benchmark for evaluating gradient-free methods against catastrophic forgetting.

The benchmark examines methods that use forward passes across multiple algorithms, forgetting scenarios, and datasets. This provides a way to study whether evaluating a model without backpropagation can support learning that preserves earlier capabilities. The authors also investigate optimization principles relevant to forgetting, conflicts between tasks, and memory requirements within this forward-pass-based setting.

The results show that forward passes alone can be sufficient to mitigate forgetting. The paper further proposes enhancements that improve resistance to forgetting without using gradients. These findings establish a possibility supported by the evaluated methods and settings, rather than a guarantee that every gradient-free procedure will succeed. The contribution combines evaluation tools with evidence and method improvements for continual learning when gradients are unavailable.
icml-2025-zeroflow-overcoming-catastroph.tldr: ZeroFlow benchmarks gradient-free continual learning and shows that forward-pass-based methods can mitigate catastrophic forgetting.
